messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes 
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)
- Forbidden causal connections that must never appear

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT include inactive components — these are clinically irrelevant for this patient and must not be mentioned.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- For forbidden pairs, never use explicit causal language between them in a single sentence:
  "led to", "caused", "as a result of", "because of", "driven by", "resulting in".
  Both components may appear in the same paragraph — just not causally linked in one sentence.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Threat: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Patel is a 29-year-old architect who came to treatment after months of telling himself he should simply be able to “get on with it.” He had arrived in the United States as a refugee in his late teens after fleeing political violence in South Asia. When he describes the event that still grips him, he returns to one day at a government checkpoint near a transit terminal where he and other civilians were being processed in a dense, pressing crowd. Men in uniform shouted contradictory orders. People were packed shoulder to shoulder, the heat and noise rising, and every delay seemed to change the mood of the soldiers. Arjun remembers watching the line stop without explanation, hearing sudden shouting and metal striking metal, and feeling the crush of bodies around him as everyone tried to read the faces of armed officials for some sign of what would happen next. What remains most potent is not only fear, but the sense that those controlling the space could do anything and no one who should have protected them was coming.

In the years since, the ordinary environments of his adult life as an architect have taken on that same charged quality. He is especially unsettled in crowded elevators at work, in packed subway platforms on site visits, and in government buildings or transit hubs whose long corridors and bottlenecks echo the place where he was trapped. Seeing security guards, police officers, or anyone in uniform immediately sharpens his attention. Loud, abrupt sounds on construction sites—a dropped steel beam, a slammed door, a radio crackling unexpectedly—make him snap upright and scan the whole room. If a client meeting is delayed, if a train stalls in a tunnel, if a line stops moving, his mind jumps quickly to danger; he assumes something bad is unfolding just out of view. In those moments he does not experience himself as remembering the past so much as recognizing a pattern he believes he has already learned to fear.

Arjun has come to believe that the institutions meant to keep people safe are unreliable at best and actively threatening at worst. That conviction makes certain places feel dangerous before anything has happened: government offices, transportation terminals, crowded lobbies, anywhere controlled by barriers, lines, and officials. He notices himself tensing on the way there, already keyed up by the expectation that he will be trapped, ignored, or overpowered. He also speaks bitterly about his own body, saying it behaves like an enemy, surging into alarm even when he knows he is in Boston and not back there. The fact that his chest tightens, his hearing sharpens, and his eyes keep darting for exits seems to him like proof that safety is never fully real. When that vigilance takes over, it deepens his despair; he thinks, with a flatness that worries him, that life narrowed to this constant bracing may not be worth much.

Over time he has organized his days around trying not to set any of this off. At work he volunteers for design tasks he can do from his desk and quietly avoids site visits that involve security screening or large groups. He takes stairs rather than crowded elevators, arrives early to meetings to avoid entering a full room, and will circle a block rather than pass a cluster of police officers. He puts considerable effort into not thinking about the checkpoint at all, cutting off images as soon as they begin. Yet the more he tries to force the memories away and keep to “safe” circumstances, the more convinced he becomes that the world really is full of hidden threats and that he is too damaged to meet them. Each new avoidance feels sensible in the moment, but afterward he reads it as evidence that his life has become smaller and that he cannot trust himself in ordinary situations.

This has begun to affect him professionally and socially. Colleagues have noticed that he is evasive about certain assignments, and he worries they see him as unreliable. He remains single and spends much of his free time alone, preferring the control of his apartment to restaurants, festivals, or crowded gatherings. Lately, even the anticipation of a delayed train or a building security check can make him start scanning for exits before he has entered the space. The more he searches for signs of danger, the more potent these places and uniforms feel, and the more immediate his fear becomes. He finally sought help after leaving a client visit in a municipal building when a line stopped moving and an officer stepped into view; afterward he sat in his car shaken and thought, with unusual clarity, that he could not keep living as if every bottleneck were the beginning of catastrophe. What he fears most is that this is permanent—that his body and mind will always drag him back there. What he hopes, cautiously, is to recover some sense that safety can exist and that his life might widen again.
